title: Will I lose my identity when I retire from sex work?
gist: A Sydney sex worker argues that AI's threat to Gen Z is primarily an identity crisis rather than an income crisis: when work confers social place, automation strips people of selfhood and community, not just wages. She notes her own income is 'AI resistant' and points to a visible young-person migration into trades and heritage crafts.

themes.theme: AI and the identity premium on work

insights.claim: Gen Z's anxiety about AI is framed as an identity problem rather than a wage problem: a cohort on the brink of adulthood does not know its place in the world because it does not know whether its work will matter.
insights.speaker: Tilly Lawless
insights.so_what: Points to demand for status- and belonging-substitutes (credentials, guilds, communities) as AI displaces entry-level work, not just income support.
insights.quote: a “generation who is on the brink of adulthood, who doesn’t really know what their place in the world or country is going to be, because they don’t know if their work is going to matter”
insights.locator: I was listening to an episode of the podcast Today, Explained

insights.claim: The North American model of finding fulfilment and purpose through work is presented as the specific cultural vulnerability that makes AI displacement destabilising, and the author argues the same exposure extends well beyond Americans.
insights.speaker: Tilly Lawless
insights.so_what: Societies that index identity to employment will absorb automation shocks with more political volatility than those that do not.
insights.locator: On the podcast, one guest spoke about how North Americans

insights.claim: Sex work is characterised as an AI-resistant income stream, and the author says she has never been more grateful that her work and therefore income sits outside automation's reach.
insights.speaker: Tilly Lawless
insights.so_what: A reminder that embodied, presence-based services are the residual moat as cognitive work is automated.
insights.quote: I’ve never been more grateful that my work (and therefore income) is AI resistant
insights.locator: I speak to a lot of people now who are turning

insights.claim: Young people are visibly retraining into trades and reviving near-extinct handicrafts such as cobbling, bookbinding and lacemaking, a shift the author is observing first-hand in her social circle.
insights.speaker: Tilly Lawless
insights.so_what: Watch for a durable bid under artisanal/trade skills and direct-from-maker commerce as AI compresses white-collar entry paths.
insights.locator: I speak to a lot of people now who are turning towards crafts

insights.claim: Asking people “how do you make your money” rather than “what do you do” reliably exposes hidden side jobs and family financial support that the status-signalling question conceals.
insights.speaker: Tilly Lawless
insights.so_what: A practical survey heuristic: headline occupation data understates the scale of portfolio income and family transfers propping up younger cohorts.
insights.quote: I usually ask them how they make their money
insights.locator: One of the first questions people tend to ask

themes.theme: Obsolescence and the fate of the unneeded

insights.claim: When an occupation disappears, the community and identity attached to it are lost with it, a pattern the author traces through knocker-uppers of the Industrial Revolution and paper boys.
insights.speaker: Tilly Lawless
insights.so_what: Social infrastructure, not just earnings, is destroyed by technological displacement, which is what turns it into political risk.
insights.locator: I think of all the jobs that have vanished

insights.claim: The turnspit dog, used for centuries to turn roasting meat and then discarded once technology advanced, is offered as a parable for how societies treat those judged to have lost their usefulness — the only surviving trace is one stuffed specimen in Abergavenny Museum in Wales.
insights.speaker: Tilly Lawless
insights.so_what: Frames the political core of the AI debate: fear of expendability, which drives demands for protection and redistribution.
insights.locator: I think of the turnspit dog

insights.claim: Leaving a profession erodes not just income but membership: the author reports already losing access to community and solidarity simply by moving from in-house brothel work to independent work after 13 years in the trade.
insights.speaker: Tilly Lawless
insights.so_what: Illustrates how gig-ification of any sector quietly dissolves the peer networks that stabilise workers.
insights.locator: I’ve done sex work for more than 13 years
